Progress on vaccinations and strong policy support are lifting activity and employment, and the Fed is maintaining an accommodative stance (0–0.25% policy rate and ongoing Treasury/MBS purchases) while monitoring virus-related risks.

SLOOS (July 2021) indicates improving credit supply and demand, reinforcing this positive backdrop:
- Banks reported stronger demand for C&I loans across large, middle‑market, and small firms, alongside higher borrower inquiries.
- Banks eased terms for C&I loans and eased standards across consumer categories (credit card, auto, and other consumer loans).
- Foreign banks also reported stronger C&I loan demand, citing financing needs for inventories, accounts receivable, plant/equipment, and M&A.
- Residential mortgage lending saw easing in some categories (with GSE‑eligible largely unchanged), and multifamily CRE standards eased; subprime originations remained limited.

Balancing this broader credit easing against ongoing virus risks and the May 2021 Financial Stability Report’s notes of elevated asset valuations and vulnerabilities in parts of nonbank finance, the tone shifts from mildly positive to moderately positive but still cautious.
